edges.effect_quant: In the Northern Manhattan Study, fasting homocysteine at or above 15 micromol/L was associated with an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.01 for ischemic stroke versus less than 10 micromol/L. In pooled prospective data, each 5 micromol/L higher homocysteine carried an odds ratio of 1.59 for stroke, and in Hordaland the oldest adults showed a graded rise in cardiovascular hospitalization risk from homocysteine 15 to 19.9 micromol/L and above 20 micromol/L.
edges.population: middle-aged and older adults, especially those with mild to moderate fasting homocysteine elevation
edges.mechanism: Higher homocysteine can impair endothelial nitric-oxide signaling, increase oxidative stress, and tilt hemostasis toward thrombosis. That makes a stroke-focused signal plausible even when homocysteine also reflects folate, B12, renal, and broader metabolic status.
edges.summary: The strongest direct anchor for this edge is the Northern Manhattan cohort, where homocysteine at or above 15 micromol/L marked a materially higher ischemic stroke risk. Older meta-analytic and population-cohort data point in the same direction, so the most defensible reading is that clearly elevated homocysteine is a harmful vascular risk marker, with stroke among the more reproducible outcomes.
edges.caveats: Homocysteine is not a pure causal toxin because it also tracks renal function, vitamin status, age, and general cardiometabolic burden. The edge is stronger as a risk signal than as proof that every homocysteine-lowering intervention will proportionally reduce stroke events.
